must_remember: Diffraction is fundamentally the interference of a continuous infinity of coherent secondary wavelets originating from the unobstructed portions of a single wavefront.
Fresnel diffraction involves finite distances for source and/or screen, producing spherical or cylindrical wavefronts.
Fraunhofer diffraction requires both source and screen to be effectively at infinite distances, realized using lenses to handle planar wavefronts.
The condition for secondary minima in single-slit diffraction is $a \sin \theta = m\lambda$, where $m = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$.
The linear width of the central maximum on a screen placed at the focal plane of a converging lens is given by $\beta_0 = \frac{2f\lambda}{a}$.
Unlike interference fringes, single-slit diffraction subsidiary maxima fall off rapidly in intensity and the central maximum is twice as wide.

glossary.meaning: Diffraction phenomenon where source, obstacle, or screen are at finite distances, resulting in spherical or cylindrical wavefronts.
Diffraction phenomenon where both source and observation screen are effectively at infinite distances, with planar incident and emergent wavefronts.
The aperture dimension through which light passes in single-slit diffraction experiments.
The angular spread from the center of the diffraction pattern to the first secondary minimum, approximated as $\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{a}$.
